questions.question: Which HTML5 element represents introductory content or navigational aids for its nearest sectioning ancestor?
questions.explanation: <header> is meant for introductory content and navigation aids for its parent section. <head> holds document metadata, <title> supplies the document title, and <section> is only a generic sectioning element.

questions.question: Which element marks a self-contained composition that could be independently distributed, such as a blog post?
questions.explanation: <article> denotes content that makes sense on its own, such as a forum post or news item. <section> merely groups related content, while <div> and <span> carry no semantic meaning at all.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is intended for content tangentially related to the content around it, such as a sidebar?
questions.explanation: <aside> is defined for tangential content like sidebars and pull quotes. <footer> closes a section, <nav> holds navigation links, and <main> is reserved for the dominant content of the page.

questions.question: Which element should wrap the dominant content of the body of an HTML document?
questions.explanation: <main> identifies the dominant content of the document body and should appear once per page. <article>, <header>, and <aside> describe specific sub-parts rather than the primary content.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is designed to contain a set of navigation links?
questions.explanation: <nav> identifies a block of navigation links and creates a navigation landmark for assistive technology. <section> is generic, <header> is introductory content, and <aside> is tangential content.

questions.question: Which element represents a footer for its nearest sectioning content or sectioning root?
questions.explanation: <footer> supplies a footer for its nearest sectioning ancestor and may contain authorship or copyright data. <bottom> is not an HTML element, <aside> is tangential, and <summary> labels a details disclosure.

questions.question: Which attribute provides a machine-readable date or time for a time element?
questions.explanation: The datetime attribute carries a machine-readable value while the text is human-readable. data-date is a custom attribute, value is used by form controls and meters, and content is a meta attribute.

questions.question: Which input type restricts entry to an email address and may show a specialised mobile keyboard?
questions.explanation: type='email' triggers browser validation and an email-oriented virtual keyboard. type='text' offers no such checking, while type='mail' and type='address' are not valid HTML input types.

questions.question: Which attribute makes a form field mandatory before the form can be submitted?
questions.explanation: The Boolean required attribute makes a control mandatory and is exposed to assistive technology. mandatory, validate, and needed are not recognised HTML attributes on form controls.

questions.question: Which meta tag sets the viewport to the device width with an initial scale of one?
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag with width=device-width and initial-scale=1 makes layouts render at device width. charset declares encoding, description is for search snippets, and http-equiv is not used for viewport settings.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element embeds scalable vector graphics directly in a document?
questions.explanation: <svg> defines vector graphics whose shapes remain crisp at any zoom level. <canvas> draws raster pixel graphics via script, <image> is not a standard HTML element, and <picture> selects bitmap sources.

questions.question: Which prefix is used for custom attributes private to a page or application?
questions.explanation: Attributes beginning with data- are valid custom data attributes accessible through element.dataset. The aria- prefix is reserved for accessibility metadata, while custom- and meta- are not defined prefixes.

questions.question: Which element provides a caption for a table?
questions.explanation: <caption> must be the first child of a table and names that table. <legend> labels a fieldset, <title> names the document, and <header> is introductory content, not a table caption.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type selects a local date and time without a time zone?
questions.explanation: datetime-local is the standard input type for a date and time with no time-zone offset. The old datetime type was removed from HTML5, and date-time and time-date are not valid input types.

questions.question: Which attribute of audio and video starts playback automatically?
questions.explanation: autoplay begins playback when enough data is available, though browsers usually require muted sound. loop repeats playback, controls shows UI, and preload only hints how much media to buffer.

questions.question: Which element inside picture specifies alternative image sources for different widths or pixel ratios?
questions.explanation: elements inside provide media and srcset candidates that the browser evaluates in order. is the fallback rendered element,

questions.question: Which attribute of a label element associates it with a specific form control?
questions.explanation: The for attribute must match the id of the associated control so clicking the label focuses it. name is submitted with form data, target is for links and forms, and aria-control is not a standard attribute.

questions.question: Which element represents a term in a description list?
questions.explanation: <dt> defines a term inside a <dl>, followed by <dd> for its description. <dl> is the list container, <dd> holds the definition, and <li> belongs to ordered and unordered lists instead.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element represents a dialog box or interactive window?
questions.explanation: <dialog> is the native element for modal and non-modal dialogs with showModal() and open behaviour. modal, popup, and window are not HTML elements for this purpose in the standard.

questions.question: Which input attribute sets the minimum number of characters a user may enter?
questions.explanation: minlength enforces a minimum character count during constraint validation. maxlength caps the count, pattern checks a regular expression, and size only suggests the visible field width.

questions.question: Which element supplies a caption or legend for the contents of a figure?
questions.explanation: <figcaption> provides a caption for its parent <figure>. <caption> belongs to tables, <legend> to fieldsets, and <summary> to details disclosures, so each has a different parent requirement.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is a generic container with no semantic meaning?
questions.explanation: <div> is a purely presentational or scripting hook with no semantic value. <section>, <article>, and <main> all convey document structure to browsers and assistive technology.

questions.question: Which attribute of an iframe specifies the URL of the page to embed?
questions.explanation: src holds the URL loaded into the iframe. href is used by links, srcdoc supplies inline HTML instead of a URL, and name identifies the frame as a browsing context target.

questions.question: Which element exposes a summary, caption, or legend for a details element?
questions.explanation: <summary> is the clickable heading that toggles its parent <details>. caption, legend, and label serve tables, fieldsets, and form controls respectively, not disclosure widgets.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type is used to choose a colour?
questions.explanation: type='color' opens the browser colour picker and returns a seven-character hex value. picker, rgb, and swatch are not valid input types in the HTML specification.

questions.question: Which attribute on a button specifies that it submits its associated form?
questions.explanation: type='submit' is the default button behaviour and triggers form submission. method and action are form attributes, while type='default' is not a valid button type value.

questions.question: Which statement about the HTML5 document outline algorithm is correct?
options: Every section automatically resets heading levels to h1 in all browsers.
The outline algorithm was never widely implemented, so authors should use explicit heading levels.
Each section must always begin with an h1 element.
Nesting sections always creates a new outline exposed to assistive technology.
questions.explanation: Browsers and screen readers never implemented the outline algorithm reliably, so real heading levels must be authored. Sections do not reset levels automatically, are not required to start with h1, and do not create exposed outlines.

questions.question: What is the effect of the global hidden attribute on an HTML element?
options: It permanently removes the element node from the DOM.
It sets display:none and prevents CSS from ever showing the element.
It applies display:none by default, which CSS may override, and removes it from the accessibility tree.
It hides the element only from screen readers while keeping it visible.
questions.explanation: hidden maps to display:none in the UA stylesheet and can be overridden by author CSS, while display:none also removes the element from the accessibility tree. It does not delete nodes and is not screen-reader-only hiding.

questions.question: Which rule does the HTML specification give for multiple main elements in one document?
options: Multiple visible main elements are allowed if each sits inside a different article.
A main element may be nested freely inside an article or section.
There must be only one main element without the hidden attribute per document.
Main is synonymous with section and may appear any number of times.
questions.explanation: The spec states that a document must not contain more than one main element that is not hidden. Nesting main inside article is invalid, and main is not interchangeable with the generic section element.

questions.question: How are subtitle text tracks attached to a video element?
options: With a track child element using kind='subtitles'
With a subtitles attribute on the video element
With a source element whose type is text/vtt
With an aria-subtitles attribute on the video element
questions.explanation: A track element with kind='subtitles', src, srclang, and label is placed inside video to expose captions or subtitles. There is no subtitles attribute, source is for media resources, and aria-subtitles is not defined.

questions.question: Which statement about the contenteditable global attribute is accurate?
options: It turns the element into a form control submitted with the form.
It may only be applied to div and span elements.
It automatically sanitises any HTML pasted into the element.
It makes content user-editable, with true, false, and inherit controlling the behaviour.
questions.explanation: contenteditable accepts true, false, and inherit and enables inline editing on any element. It does not create a form control, is not restricted to two tags, and performs no sanitisation of pasted markup.

questions.question: What is the status of the scoped attribute on a style element in modern HTML?
options: It limits styles to the parent element and is supported by all major browsers.
It was removed from the specification and has no effect in modern browsers.
It creates a new stacking context for the styled element.
It applies styles only when the style element is inside the head.
questions.explanation: The scoped attribute was dropped from the HTML specification and never gained broad implementation. It does not scope CSS, influence stacking, or depend on whether the style element sits in head or body.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls the space between an element's content and its border?
questions.explanation: padding adds space inside the border around the content box. margin adds space outside the border, gap separates grid or flex tracks, and spacing is not a CSS property.

questions.question: Which CSS property sets the foreground text colour of an element?
questions.explanation: color sets the foreground colour used by text and currentColor. background-color paints behind content, font-style selects italic or normal, and color-scheme hints light or dark UA rendering.

questions.question: In the CSS box model, which property adds space outside the border of an element?
questions.explanation: margin is the transparent area outside the border that separates elements. padding is inside the border, border itself is the edge, and content is the innermost box rather than a spacing property.

questions.question: Which declaration makes an element's declared width include its padding and border?
questions.explanation: box-sizing: border-box makes width and height cover content, padding, and border. content-box excludes padding and border, and the other two values do not exist in CSS.

questions.question: Which CSS property distributes flex items along the main axis of a flex container?
questions.explanation: justify-content aligns flex items along the main axis. align-items and align-content work on the cross axis, and place-self aligns a single item within its own grid or flex area.

questions.question: Which display value turns an element into a flex container?
questions.explanation: display:flex establishes a flex formatting context for the element's children. display:grid creates a grid context, block is the normal block flow, and table emulates legacy table layout.

questions.question: Which CSS property allows a flex item to absorb extra free space?
questions.explanation: flex-grow defines the factor by which an item receives leftover main-axis space. flex-shrink controls shrinking, flex-basis sets the initial size, and align-self adjusts cross-axis alignment.

questions.question: Which CSS property defines a grid using named template areas?
questions.explanation: grid-template-areas draws named regions with strings of area names. grid-template-columns sizes tracks, grid-area places an item into a named area, and grid-auto-flow controls auto-placement direction.

questions.question: Which pseudo-element selects the first line of a block of text?
questions.explanation: ::first-line styles the first rendered line of a block container. ::first-letter styles one character, ::before inserts generated content, and ::marker styles list bullets or numbers.

questions.question: Which selector targets an element with class active inside a nav element?
questions.explanation: nav .active is a descendant selector matching any .active inside a nav. nav.active means one element with both names, nav > active is a child type selector, and .active nav reverses the relationship.

questions.question: Which CSS property paints a shadow outside an element's box?
questions.explanation: box-shadow adds one or more shadows to an element's box. text-shadow only affects glyphs, drop-shadow is a filter function rather than a property, and border-shadow does not exist.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls the paint order of positioned elements?
questions.explanation: z-index sets the stack level of a positioned element within its stacking context. position establishes the positioning scheme, overflow clips content, and float shifts boxes in flow.

questions.question: Which CSS unit is relative to the root element's font size?
questions.explanation: rem always resolves against the root html font size. em resolves against the current element's parent font size, percentages depend on the property, and px is an absolute CSS pixel length.

questions.question: Given #nav a { color: blue; } and .link { color: red; }, which rule colours <a id='nav' class='link'>?
options: #nav a, because an ID selector gives it higher specificity
.link, because class rules are evaluated after descendant rules
Neither rule applies, because the type selector cancels both
Both apply equally, so the rule declared last always wins
questions.explanation: The #nav a selector has specificity 1-0-1 versus 0-1-0 for .link, so blue wins regardless of source order. Classes do not automatically win later, type selectors do not cancel declarations, and source order only breaks specificity ties.

questions.question: Which declaration centres a flex item both horizontally and vertically in its container?
options: justify-items: center; align-items: center; on the container
text-align: center; vertical-align: middle; on the container
place-content: center alone on the container
display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; on the container
questions.explanation: justify-content centres on the main axis and align-items on the cross axis of a flex container. justify-items is a grid property, text-align only aligns inline content, and place-content without a flex or grid context has no effect.

questions.question: Which CSS property changes the visual order of flex items without changing the DOM?
questions.explanation: order reorders flex or grid items visually while source order stays intact, which can harm keyboard flow if overused. flex-direction flips the whole axis, z-index changes painting order, and grid-row is grid-only placement.

questions.question: Which CSS property allows flex items to be placed on multiple lines?
questions.explanation: flex-wrap: wrap lets items move onto new lines when the main axis is full. flex-flow-wrap and wrap are not valid properties, and white-space affects text wrapping inside a single line of text, not flex items.

questions.question: Which CSS function paints a repeating pattern of linear colour stops?
questions.explanation: repeating-linear-gradient() tiles its stop list indefinitely to form stripes. linear-gradient() paints one gradient, radial-gradient() radiates from a centre, and a bare gradient() function does not exist in CSS.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls how a background image is sized within its element?
questions.explanation: background-size accepts lengths, percentages, cover, and contain to scale a background image. background-position moves it, background-repeat tiles it, and background-attachment fixes or scrolls it relative to the viewport.

questions.question: What does transition: all 0.3s ease declare?
options: It starts a keyframe animation as soon as the page loads.
It delays all CSS parsing by 0.3 seconds.
It animates changes to animatable properties over 0.3 seconds with easing.
It disables transitions for all properties except ease.
questions.explanation: A transition interpolates between old and new computed values of animatable properties when a change occurs, here over 0.3s with an ease timing function. It is not an animation trigger, parser delay, or disabling rule.

questions.question: Which CSS at-rule defines named keyframes for an animation?
questions.explanation: @keyframes declares named stages such as from and to that an animation property references. @media applies conditional styles, @supports tests feature availability, and @import loads another stylesheet.

questions.question: Which declaration rotates an element by 45 degrees?
questions.explanation: rotate() takes an angle with a unit such as deg, so rotate(45deg) is valid. A unitless 45 is invalid, turn() is not a transform function, and rotateX() rotates around the horizontal axis in 3D instead.

questions.question: Which is a valid way to define and reuse a CSS custom property?
questions.explanation: Custom properties are declared with a double-hyphen name and read with var(--name), commonly on :root. The dollar syntax belongs to Sass, and the equals-sign and bare var forms are invalid CSS.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls whether an element can be interactively resized?
questions.explanation: resize allows or disallows user resizing of elements whose overflow is not visible. overflow controls clipping and scrollbars, user-select controls text selection, and zoom scales rendering rather than enabling a resize handle.

questions.question: What is the behaviour of position: sticky?
options: The element is fixed to the viewport from the very start.
It acts like relative positioning until a threshold is crossed, then sticks like fixed.
The element is always painted behind its siblings.
The element can no longer be scrolled with the page.
questions.explanation: A sticky box stays in normal flow until its scroll container reaches the specified offset, then remains pinned. It is not fixed initially, does not alter paint order, and still scrolls with its container.

questions.question: Which CSS property creates a multi-column text layout?
questions.explanation: column-count splits content into the requested number of balanced columns. grid-template-columns defines grid tracks, flex-direction sets a flex axis, and column-gap only sets spacing between existing columns.

questions.question: Which statement about CSS stacking contexts is accurate?
options: A positioned element with a z-index other than auto creates a stacking context for its descendants.
z-index affects every element even when position is static.
opacity: 1 always establishes a new stacking context.
transform: none always creates a stacking context.
questions.explanation: Positioned elements with a numeric z-index establish a stacking context whose children stack only within it. Static elements ignore z-index, and only opacity below 1 or an actual transform value creates a context.

questions.question:
With .a { color: red !important; } and #id p { color: blue; }, what colour is

?
options: blue, because the ID selector has higher specificity
Neither colour, because the declaration is invalid
red, because !important overrides normal declarations regardless of specificity
blue, because descendant selectors outrank class selectors
questions.explanation: An important declaration wins over any normal declaration, so higher ID specificity cannot beat it. The declaration is valid, and descendant combinators do not automatically outrank classes in the cascade.

questions.question: Why can a descendant read a custom property declared on an ancestor?
options: Custom properties are not inherited at all and require JavaScript.
The inherit keyword must be written on every custom property use.
Custom properties inherit by default, and a local redeclaration on the descendant overrides the value.
Only variables declared on :root are visible to descendants.
questions.explanation: Custom properties follow normal inheritance, so descendants resolve them unless they redeclare the variable locally. No inherit keyword or JavaScript is required, and they may be declared on any element, not just :root.

questions.question: What does grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) produce?
options: As many flexible columns of at least 200px as fit, sharing extra space equally
Exactly two fixed 200px columns regardless of container width
A single column that always overflows the container
Columns that are always exactly 200px wide with no growth
questions.explanation: auto-fit repeats the track list as often as it fits, and minmax(200px, 1fr) lets each track grow beyond 200px to absorb free space. It is not a fixed two-column rule, and tracks do not overflow when sized correctly.

questions.question: Which selector has the highest specificity: #main .item:hover, .item.active::before, or body #main > ul li?
options: All three selectors have identical specificity
questions.explanation: #main .item:hover is 1-2-0, body #main > ul li is 1-0-3, and .item.active::before is 0-2-1. ID counts outrank class counts, so the first wins; they are not equal and neither of the others has more IDs.

questions.question: Why is transform: translateZ(0) sometimes used as a rendering hint?
options: It reduces the opacity of the element to zero.
It can promote the element to its own compositor layer, reducing repaints during animation.
It guarantees hardware acceleration in every browser and device.
It disables hardware acceleration to conserve battery power.
questions.explanation: A 3D transform may cause the browser to promote an element to a composited layer, so animation can avoid repeated layout and paint. It does not change opacity, is only a hint rather than a guarantee, and does not disable acceleration.

questions.question: What does width=device-width accomplish in a viewport meta tag?
options: It forces the page into landscape orientation.
It matches the layout viewport width to the device screen width in CSS pixels.
It limits the page to a fixed 980 pixel canvas.
questions.explanation: width=device-width makes the layout viewport equal to the device width in CSS pixels so media queries reflect the real screen. It does not set orientation, impose a 980px canvas, or disable zoom.

questions.question: Which CSS at-rule applies styles only when viewport conditions are met?
questions.explanation: @media contains rules that apply when a media query matches, such as a minimum width. @keyframes defines animation steps, @font-face declares fonts, and @supports tests CSS feature support instead.

questions.question: What does a mobile-first CSS approach mean?
options: Write base styles for small screens and add enhancements with min-width queries.
Design only for phones and ignore larger devices.
Use only fixed pixel widths for predictable layouts.
Write only max-width queries with no base styles at all.
questions.explanation: Mobile-first starts with a simple small-screen baseline and layers on features as width grows via min-width queries. It does not exclude other devices, require fixed widths, or forbid a sensible baseline.

questions.question: Which CSS unit equals one percent of the viewport width?
questions.explanation: 1vw is one percent of the viewport width and changes when the viewport resizes. vh is based on height, while em and rem are font-relative units that ignore viewport dimensions.

questions.question: Which CSS unit equals one percent of the viewport height?
questions.explanation: 1vh resolves to one percent of the viewport height. vw is width-based, ch is the width of a zero glyph, and pt is an absolute physical length rather than a viewport-relative one.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute offers the browser candidate image files for different densities or widths?
questions.explanation: srcset lists image URL candidates with width or density descriptors so the browser can pick one. src is the fallback URL, sizes describes display width, and data-src is a custom lazy-loading hook.

questions.question: Which element acts as an art-direction container for different images at different breakpoints?
questions.explanation: picture holds source elements with media queries plus a fallback img for art direction. img alone cannot swap compositions by media query, figure is only a caption wrapper, and canvas is script-drawn raster output.

questions.question: Which CSS function limits a value between a minimum and a maximum?
questions.explanation: clamp(min, preferred, max) returns the preferred value bounded by min and max. minmax() sizes grid tracks, calc() evaluates expressions without bounding, and fit-content() clamps to available content size in track sizing.

questions.question: In a responsive image, what does the sizes attribute describe?
options: The maximum download size in kilobytes
The intended display width of the image under given viewport conditions
The number of source files available
The intrinsic height of the image file
questions.explanation: sizes gives the browser the layout width of the image, often as a media-condition and length list, so it can choose from srcset. It is not a byte limit, a file count, or an intrinsic dimension.

questions.question: Which CSS declaration scales an image down inside its container while preserving its aspect ratio?
questions.explanation: max-width:100% with height:auto lets an image shrink on narrow screens without stretching or distorting. Setting both dimensions can distort it, object-fit:fill stretches, and overflow:hidden only clips.

questions.question: Which media feature detects a user's preference for a dark colour scheme?
questions.explanation: prefers-color-scheme: dark matches when the user has requested a dark theme. prefers-reduced-motion concerns animation, color-scheme is a CSS property for UA rendering, and dark-mode is not a media feature.

questions.question: What is a breakpoint in responsive web design?
options: The moment the page finishes loading
A universally fixed width of 1024 pixels
A viewport threshold where the layout changes via a media query
A CSS unit equal to eight pixels
questions.explanation: A breakpoint is a chosen viewport width at which styles change to suit available space. It is not a load event, not fixed to one device width, and not a CSS unit.

questions.question: Which media query targets viewports at least 768 pixels wide?
questions.explanation: min-width:768px matches viewports equal to or wider than 768px. max-width matches narrower ones, min-device-width refers to physical screen size, and the or form is not valid media query syntax.

questions.question: What does 1rem equal with the browser's default settings?
options: The root html font size, normally 16 pixels
The font size of the immediate parent element
One percent of the viewport height
questions.explanation: rem is relative to the root element font size, typically 16px by default. It is not parent-relative like em, has no fixed 10px definition, and has no relationship to viewport height.

questions.question: How does em differ from rem when used for font-size?
options: em is always relative to the root and rem to the parent.
They are synonyms in modern CSS.
em is an absolute unit while rem is relative.
em is relative to the parent element's font size and rem to the root element's font size.
questions.explanation: em compounds against the inherited font size of the parent, whereas rem always refers to the root font size. They are not interchangeable, and neither is an absolute unit.

questions.question: Which declaration creates fluid type that scales with the viewport but stays between 16px and 24px?
questions.explanation: clamp(min, preferred, max) with 1rem + 1vw scales fluidly while enforcing 16px and 24px bounds. The first choice reverses the bounds, fluid() is not a CSS function, and calc() only adds fixed lengths.

questions.question: Which declaration creates as many grid columns as fit, each at least 250px wide?
questions.explanation: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) adds tracks while each stays at least 250px and shares spare space. The other forms misuse argument order or invent properties that CSS does not define.

questions.question: Which declaration creates a grid container with a 16px gap between tracks?
options: gap: 16px only works in flexbox, not grid.
grid-gap is the only property accepted by browsers.
questions.explanation: gap sets row and column gutters in both grid and flex layouts once display:grid is applied. grid-gap is a legacy alias rather than the only option, and spacing is not a CSS property.

questions.question: Which CSS property specifies the intrinsic aspect ratio of a replaced element such as an image?
questions.explanation: aspect-ratio accepts a ratio such as 16 / 10 and reserves space before media loads. ratio, object-ratio, and image-ratio are not defined CSS properties.

questions.question: What is the purpose of viewport-fit=cover in a viewport meta tag?
options: It disables zooming on all devices.
It forces the page into landscape orientation.
It allows content to extend into the safe areas of notched displays.
It forces a one-to-one device pixel ratio.
questions.explanation: viewport-fit=cover lets layout extend behind notches and rounded corners, after which safe-area-inset variables should pad content. It does not control zoom, orientation, or device pixel ratio.

questions.question: Which declaration prevents a flex item from shrinking at all when space is tight?
questions.explanation: flex-shrink:0 keeps an item at its flex-basis instead of reducing it. flex-grow:0 only stops growth, flex-basis:auto sets the starting size, and min-width:0 actually permits shrinking below content size.

questions.question: Which practice helps prevent a horizontal scrollbar on narrow screens?
options: Use max-width:100% on images together with box-sizing:border-box
Use fixed-width tables for all content
Set the body width to 980 pixels
Remove all media queries from the stylesheet
questions.explanation: Fluid images and border-box sizing keep content inside the viewport. Fixed tables, a hard 980px body, and removing media queries all make overflow more likely on small screens.

questions.question: Which CSS function evaluates an expression such as 100% minus 2rem?
questions.explanation: calc() performs arithmetic on CSS lengths, percentages, and units. clamp() bounds a value, while min() and max() select the smallest or largest among arguments rather than computing an expression.

questions.question: What does the media feature (hover: hover) detect?
options: Whether the device is a mobile phone
Whether the primary input mechanism can hover over elements
Whether the screen has a high pixel density
Whether JavaScript is enabled in the browser
questions.explanation: hover:hover matches when the primary pointing device can hover, which helps tune hover-dependent UI. It says nothing about phone classification, pixel density, or scripting support.

questions.question: What is the difference between the prefers-color-scheme media query and the color-scheme CSS property?
options: They are exact aliases and can be used interchangeably.
The query detects the OS preference so authors can write styles; the property declares which schemes the page supports so UA styles adapt.
The property only works when called from JavaScript.
The query only affects meta tags and cannot style elements.
questions.explanation: prefers-color-scheme is a media feature for detecting the user's theme choice, while color-scheme tells the browser which schemes the document supports so form controls and scrollbars adapt. They are not aliases, are not JS-only, and the query styles real elements.

questions.question: Why is a hard min-width: 320px on the body discouraged in responsive design?
options: It makes every media query evaluate correctly.
It permanently disables zooming on phones.
It forces horizontal scrolling on narrower viewports instead of letting the layout adapt.
questions.explanation: A fixed minimum body width makes content wider than viewports below 320px, producing horizontal scrolling rather than adaptation. It does not help assistive technology, ensure query accuracy, or control zoom behaviour.

questions.question: How does a browser choose between 1x and 2x srcset candidates when sizes is omitted?
options: It uses the device pixel ratio to pick an appropriately dense candidate.
It downloads every listed candidate and renders the largest.
It ignores the srcset attribute entirely without sizes.
It always uses the first candidate regardless of display density.
questions.explanation: Density descriptors such as 1x and 2x are matched against the device pixel ratio when the browser picks a source. It does not fetch all candidates, does not require sizes for density selection, and does not blindly take the first URL.

questions.question: What happens when the preferred value of clamp(MIN, VAL, MAX) lies outside the bounds?
options: The browser raises a CSS parsing error.
The result is MIN when VAL is smaller and MAX when VAL is larger.
The declaration falls back to the inherited value.
questions.explanation: clamp resolves to MIN if the preferred value is below it and to MAX if above it, keeping results inside the interval. It never becomes zero, is valid CSS, and does not fall back to inheritance.

questions.question: Which approach best limits layout shift caused by late-loading web fonts?
options: Banning all web fonts is the only possible remedy.
Using font-display: block with no fallback face at all.
Using font-display: swap or optional with a metric-adjusted fallback via size-adjust.
Injecting the font stylesheet with JavaScript after first paint.
questions.explanation: A metric-compatible fallback plus size-adjust reduces the reflow when the real font arrives, and font-display controls the swap behaviour. Banning fonts is unnecessary, blocking with no fallback delays text, and late JS injection worsens the shift.

questions.question: In CSS Grid, what does grid-column: 2 / span 3 mean?
options: The item begins at grid line 2 and spans three tracks.
The item occupies columns 2 and 3 only.
The item starts at track 2 and finishes at track 3.
Three additional columns are inserted before the item.
questions.explanation: The slash separates start and end lines, and span 3 counts three tracks from line 2. It is not a two-column placement, not an end at line 3, and placement never creates new tracks.

questions.question: Why prefer auto-fit with minmax() over many fixed breakpoints for a card grid?
options: It removes the need to write any CSS at all.
It guarantees identical card heights in every browser.
It disables responsive images inside the cards.
The column count adapts continuously to available width, so fewer manual breakpoints are needed.
questions.explanation: An auto-fit minmax grid reflows whenever the container width changes, avoiding a long list of device-specific breakpoints. It still requires CSS, does not normalise card heights, and does not affect image selection.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that may be reassigned?
questions.explanation: let creates a block-scoped binding that can be reassigned later. const blocks reassignment, var is function-scoped and hoisted, and static is a class member keyword rather than a variable declaration.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a block-scoped binding that cannot be reassigned?
questions.explanation: const creates a block-scoped, non-reassignable binding, though object contents can still mutate. let allows reassignment, var is function-scoped, and final is not a JavaScript keyword.

questions.question: What is the value of typeof null in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: typeof null returns 'object' due to a long-standing language quirk. It is not 'null', not 'undefined', and certainly not 'boolean'; checking for null requires a strict equality test.

questions.question: Which syntax correctly declares a one-parameter arrow function that doubles its input?
questions.explanation: An arrow function uses => between parameters and body, so x => x * 2 is valid. A dash followed by >, a missing parameter, or combining function with => are all syntax errors.

questions.question: What does object destructuring do in const {name, age} = person;?
options: Creates a brand new person object with those properties.
Deletes the named properties from person.
Extracts matching properties into local variables of the same names.
Converts person into a JSON string.
questions.explanation: Destructuring reads properties from person and binds them to local const variables name and age. It neither mutates nor recreates the source object and performs no serialisation.

questions.question: What does the spread operator do in const copy = [...arr];?
options: Creates another reference pointing to the original array.
Reverses the order of the elements.
Creates a shallow copy of the elements in a new array.
Converts the array into an object with numeric keys as strings.
questions.explanation: Spreading an array into a new array literal copies its elements into a distinct shallow array. It is not an alias, does not reverse anything, and does not change the value into an object.

questions.question: Which syntax embeds an expression inside a JavaScript template literal?
questions.explanation: Template literals interpolate expressions using ${...} inside backticks. The hash, double-brace, and @ forms belong to other templating languages and have no meaning in JavaScript template literals.

questions.question: Which array method adds elements to the end and returns the array's new length?
questions.explanation: push() appends items and returns the new length. pop() removes the last item, shift() removes the first, and splice() inserts or removes at arbitrary positions while returning removed elements.

questions.question: Which syntax declares a class in ES6?
questions.explanation: The class keyword followed by a name and a body declares a class, optionally with a constructor method. The other forms mix keywords incorrectly and are syntax errors in JavaScript.

questions.question: Which keyword refers to the current instance inside a class method?
questions.explanation: Inside a class method, this refers to the object on which the method was called. super accesses the parent class, while self and that are user-defined variable names with no special meaning.

questions.question: Which statement imports the default export of the module './math.js'?
questions.explanation: A default export is imported without braces using import name from path. Braces import a named export, require is CommonJS syntax, and include is not a JavaScript statement.

questions.question: Which Promise method registers a handler for a rejected promise?
questions.explanation: catch() handles rejection, equivalent to then with a rejection handler. A lone then may handle fulfilment only, finally always runs without handling the reason, and resolve is a static constructor method.

questions.question: Which keyword suspends an async function until a promise settles?
questions.explanation: await pauses an async function until its operand settles, then resumes with the fulfilled value. yield belongs to generators, and defer and suspend are not JavaScript keywords.

questions.question: What is the temporal dead zone in JavaScript?
options: The delay between page load and the DOMContentLoaded event.
The interval during which a var binding is automatically undefined.
The region from block entry until a let or const declaration is evaluated, where access throws ReferenceError.
The delay before a setTimeout callback can run.
questions.explanation: let and const bindings exist but remain uninitialised from block entry until their declaration runs, so early access throws ReferenceError. This is unrelated to DOM readiness, var's undefined initialisation, or timer delay.

questions.question: In JavaScript, what is a closure?
options: A function that keeps access to variables from its outer scope after that scope has returned.
A function that invokes itself immediately once.
A block of statements wrapped in a try and catch.
An object whose properties cannot be enumerated.
questions.explanation: A closure is the combination of a function and its remembered lexical environment, allowing it to read outer variables later. An IIFE is a separate pattern, try/catch is error handling, and non-enumerability is unrelated.

questions.question: Which expression constructs a Set containing only unique values?
questions.explanation: new Set takes an iterable, so the array yields the unique members 1, 2, and 3. new Map expects key-value pairs, new Array creates an array, and an object literal with numeric keys is not valid iterable input.

questions.question: Which ES6 feature collects remaining function arguments into an array?
questions.explanation: A rest parameter written as ...args gathers extra arguments into a real array. Spread expands iterables at call sites, defaults supply fallback values, and destructuring unpacks structured values.

questions.question: What is the result of [1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 2)?
questions.explanation: map applies the callback to each element and returns a new array of the same length, here [2, 4, 6]. It does not drop elements, return a sum, or concatenate original and transformed values.

questions.question: Which array method returns a new array containing only elements that pass a test?
questions.explanation: filter() builds a new array of items for which the callback returns truthy. find() returns one element, some() returns a boolean, and forEach() only iterates and returns undefined.

questions.question: What does the optional chaining operator ?. do?
options: Calls a function only when that function is asynchronous.
Throws a deliberate error whenever a value is null.
Short-circuits to undefined when the value before it is null or undefined.
Coerces the following value to a boolean.
questions.explanation: Optional chaining prevents a TypeError by returning undefined when the left-hand side is nullish, and it can also guard calls. It has nothing to do with async checks, deliberate throws, or boolean coercion.

questions.question: What does a ?? b return when a is 0?
options: b, because zero is a falsy value
undefined, because zero is not a valid operand
0, because nullish coalescing only falls back on null or undefined
b, because nullish coalescing treats zero as missing
questions.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator checks only for null or undefined, so 0, false, and empty strings are preserved. That is the key difference from the || operator, which would return b for 0.

questions.question: Which built-in collection allows keys of any data type, including objects?
questions.explanation: Map stores key-value pairs using SameValueZero comparison, so functions and objects are valid keys. Set stores only values, WeakRef holds a weak object reference, and Array indexes are strings or integers.

questions.question: What does Symbol('id') return?
options: A unique string containing the text id.
An object with an id property.
A numeric identifier generated by the engine.
A unique immutable primitive value often used as a property key.
questions.explanation: Symbol creates a new unique primitive value on every call, commonly used for non-colliding property keys. It is not a string, an object, or a number, even though the description argument may be 'id'.

questions.question: What does hoisting mean in JavaScript?
options: Moving stylesheet rules to the top of a document.
Making var declarations and function declarations available before their source line, while let and const stay uninitialised until evaluated.
questions.explanation: Declarations are processed before code executes, so var is initialised to undefined and function declarations are callable early. let and const are hoisted but remain in the temporal dead zone; CSS, imports, and arrays are unrelated.

questions.question: What does export default function greet() {} permit?
options: Importing greet with a named import inside braces.
Importing it with any local name through a default import.
Using greet in another file with no import statement.
Publishing the module to a CommonJS registry only.
questions.explanation: A default export can be imported under any chosen local name because there is one default per module. Named imports require a named export, cross-file use needs an import, and ES modules are not CommonJS.

questions.question: In what order are microtasks and macrotasks processed after the call stack empties?
options: All macrotasks run first, then queued microtasks.
Tasks run strictly in insertion order regardless of category.
Only microtasks execute; macrotasks are discarded.
All queued microtasks drain first, then one macrotask runs, then microtasks drain again.
questions.explanation: The event loop drains the microtask queue completely after each task, so promise callbacks run before the next timer or I/O callback. Macrotasks do not go first, queues are not merged, and macrotasks are never discarded.

questions.question: What is the value of this in a top-level arrow function inside an ES module?
options: undefined, because modules are strict and arrows have no own this
the window object in every browser
the global object in every environment
questions.explanation: Arrow functions capture this lexically, and top-level this in an ES module is undefined because modules are strict. A classic script would have window as global this, but arrows never bind their own this.

questions.question: What does for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); print?
questions.explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three closures share one variable whose final value is 3 when timers run. Using let would create a fresh binding per iteration and print 0, 1, 2; the value is never undefined.

questions.question: Which statement about calling new Foo() on an ES6 class is correct?
options: A class can also be invoked as a plain function without new.
It creates an object with Foo.prototype as its prototype, binds this, and returns that object unless the constructor returns another object.
Class methods become enumerable own properties of each instance.
questions.explanation: The new operator allocates the instance, links its prototype, runs the constructor with this bound, and returns the object. Classes cannot be called without new, constructors do not return undefined, and methods live on the prototype.

questions.question: What does Object.freeze(obj) do?
options: Makes existing own properties non-writable and non-configurable and prevents new properties, shallowly.
Recursively freezes all nested objects as well.
Removes every property from the object.
Makes the object read-only only when strict mode is active.
questions.explanation: Object.freeze applies shallow immutability: existing own properties cannot be changed or deleted and extension is prevented. Nested objects remain mutable, no properties are removed, and the restriction applies in sloppy mode too.

questions.question: Which statement correctly swaps the values of a and b using destructuring?
options: {a, b} = {b, a} without any surrounding parentheses
questions.explanation: An array destructuring assignment evaluates the right-hand [b, a] array first, then assigns both variables, so values swap correctly. The comma form parses as separate expressions, object assignment needs parentheses, and sequential assignment loses a's value.

questions.question: Which DOM method returns the first element that matches a CSS selector?
questions.explanation: querySelector() returns the first matching element or null. getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection, querySelectorAll returns all matches, and getElementById only matches an id value.

questions.question: Which property of a DOM element returns only its element children, ignoring text nodes?
questions.explanation: children is an HTMLCollection of element nodes only. childNodes includes text and comment nodes, parentNode points upward, and there is no standard siblings property.

questions.question: Which method adds a node as the last child of an element?
questions.explanation: appendChild() places a node at the end of an element's child list and returns it. insertBefore() needs a reference node, while prependChild() and addChild() are not standard DOM methods.

questions.question: Which method removes the element itself from the DOM?
questions.explanation: Element.remove() detaches the element without needing a parent reference. detach, delete, and destroy are not DOM methods; the older alternative is parent.removeChild(child).

questions.question: Which method registers a callback to run when an event occurs on an element?
questions.explanation: addEventListener(type, handler, options) is the standard registration API. attachEvent was an old Internet Explorer method, and onEvent and listen are not defined methods.

questions.question: Which event fires when a form is submitted?
questions.explanation: The submit event is dispatched on the form element when submission is triggered. click occurs on buttons, change fires after a value commit, and input fires on each value change.

questions.question: Which property of an Event object identifies the element that originally dispatched it?
questions.explanation: event.target is the original dispatch target, which may be a child of the listener's element. currentTarget is the element whose listener is running, while source and origin are not Event properties.

questions.question: Which event fires on every keystroke that changes a text input's value?
questions.explanation: input fires immediately whenever the value changes, including each keystroke. change fires when the value is committed, submit is form-level, and blur fires when focus leaves.

questions.question: Which method cancels the browser's default action for an event?
questions.explanation: preventDefault() blocks actions such as following a link or submitting a form. stopPropagation only halts propagation, and preventBubble and cancelEvent do not exist.

questions.question: Which web storage object keeps data until it is explicitly removed, with no expiry?
questions.explanation: localStorage persists across sessions until cleared by script or the user. sessionStorage is cleared when the tab session ends, and the other names are not standard Web Storage objects.

questions.question: Which browser API performs asynchronous HTTP requests and returns a Promise?
questions.explanation: fetch() returns a Promise resolving to a Response object. XMLHttpRequest is the older callback-based API, while request() and ajax() are not built-in browser functions.

questions.question: What does document.createElement('div') return?
options: A string containing the tag name
null until the node is appended to the document
A new detached DOM element node
questions.explanation: createElement constructs a new, detached element ready to be configured and inserted. It does not return markup text, a library wrapper, or null.

questions.question: What is event bubbling?
options: An event propagates from the target element upward through its ancestors.
An event begins at the document and travels down to the target.
The event is cloned once for each child element.
The event data is written into sessionStorage.
questions.explanation: During bubbling, the event visits the target and then each ancestor in turn. The downward path is the capture phase, events are not cloned per child, and storage is not involved.

questions.question: Which third argument to addEventListener enables the capture phase?
questions.explanation: Passing true as the third argument (or {capture:true}) listens during capture. The once and passive options control invocation count and default prevention, while capture:false disables capturing.

questions.question: What does event delegation rely on to handle events from many children?
options: Attaching a separate listener to every child element.
The guarantee that each event fires only once per page.
Event bubbling, so one ancestor listener receives child events.
Inline onclick attributes on each child.
questions.explanation: Delegation places one listener on an ancestor and uses bubbling plus event.target to identify the originating child. It avoids many individual listeners, is not about firing frequency, and does not require inline handlers.

questions.question: Which method stops an event from continuing to propagate to ancestor listeners?
questions.explanation: stopPropagation() prevents further travel in the capture or bubble phase. preventDefault() cancels default browser behaviour, stopImmediateDefault does not exist, and removeEventListener detaches a handler.

questions.question: What does the once: true listener option do?
options: Makes the listener passive and non-cancellable.
Prevents the browser default action automatically.
Runs the listener only during the capture phase.
Removes the listener automatically after its first invocation.
questions.explanation: With once:true, the listener is invoked at most once and then unregistered. Passive behaviour and capture are separate options, and preventing defaults still requires preventDefault().

questions.question: Which DOM property reads or replaces the HTML markup inside an element?
questions.explanation: innerHTML parses and serialises descendant markup, so untrusted input can cause XSS. textContent treats content as plain text, outerText is non-standard, and nodeValue applies to text nodes.

questions.question: Which API returns an element's computed style after all CSS rules have been applied?
questions.explanation: window.getComputedStyle returns a live CSSStyleDeclaration with resolved values. element.style only exposes inline declarations, element.css is not defined, and styleSheets lists stylesheets rather than resolved styles.

questions.question: What does document.querySelectorAll('p') return?
options: An array of matching tag-name strings
A live NodeList that updates as the DOM changes
A static NodeList containing all matching elements
questions.explanation: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList snapshot of all matches. It is not an array of strings, does not return only one element, and unlike getElementsByTagName it does not update live.

questions.question: Which property of a DOM node refers to its immediate parent node?
questions.explanation: parentNode points to the node's immediate parent. nextSibling points forward, ownerDocument points to the containing document, and firstChild points to the first child node.

questions.question: What is CORS?
options: A CSS method for responsive images.
A JavaScript framework for building components.
A browser security mechanism using HTTP headers to permit or restrict cross-origin requests.
questions.explanation: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing uses headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin so a server can allow browsers to expose responses to other origins. It is not CSS, a framework, or a database feature.

questions.question: Which statement about fetch() is correct?
options: fetch() rejects the promise whenever the server returns a 404 status.
fetch() can only issue GET requests.
fetch() resolves with a Response even for HTTP errors such as 404; response.ok signals success.
fetch() executes synchronously and blocks rendering.
questions.explanation: fetch rejects only on network failure, so callers must inspect response.ok or status for HTTP errors. It supports all HTTP methods through the options object and is asynchronous by design.

questions.question: Which call stores a string value under the key user in localStorage?
questions.explanation: setItem(key, value) writes a string to Web Storage, retrievable with getItem. add, write, and push are not methods on the Storage interface.

questions.question: What does JSON.parse return when given a JSON string representing an object with property x equal to 1?
options: A JavaScript object with property x equal to 1
questions.explanation: JSON.parse constructs the corresponding JavaScript value, so a JSON object literal becomes a real object. It does not echo the string, return undefined, or produce null unless the input is the text null.

questions.question: What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
options: They always reference exactly the same element.
target is the original dispatching element; currentTarget is the element whose listener is executing.
target is the document and currentTarget is the window.
currentTarget exists only for keyboard events.
questions.explanation: In a delegated handler, target is the clicked descendant while currentTarget is the ancestor holding the listener. They coincide only when the listener is on the target itself, and both work for all event types.

questions.question: What does a passive event listener promise?
options: The listener will be invoked exactly once and then removed.
The listener will not call preventDefault(), letting the browser optimise scrolling.
The listener runs only in the bubble phase.
The listener is attached to the document rather than an element.
questions.explanation: passive:true tells the browser the handler will not cancel the event, enabling smoother touch and wheel scrolling. once controls repetition, capture controls phase, and attachment target is independent.

questions.question: What happens when an error is thrown inside one event listener?
options: The browser automatically retries the listener three times.
The error is always uploaded to the application server.
All future events on the page stop firing permanently.
It is reported as an uncaught exception, but other listeners for the same event still run.
questions.explanation: An exception in one listener is reported to the global error handling mechanism and does not abort dispatch to remaining listeners. There is no automatic retry or upload, and the page keeps handling events.

questions.question: Which API observes additions, removals, and attribute changes in the DOM tree?
questions.explanation: MutationObserver delivers records when the observed DOM subtree changes. IntersectionObserver tracks viewport visibility, ResizeObserver tracks element size, and PerformanceObserver listens for performance entries.

questions.question: Which technique avoids attaching hundreds of handlers to list items?
options: Attaching one handler to every item during a loop.
Writing an inline onclick for each item.
Event delegation with a single listener on a common ancestor.
Polling with setInterval to detect clicks.
questions.explanation: Delegation uses bubbling so one ancestor handler serves current and future children, reducing memory and setup cost. Per-item handlers and inline attributes scale poorly, and polling is wasteful and inaccurate.

questions.question: What does Element.closest('.card') return?
options: All descendants that have the class card
The nearest ancestor, or the element itself, matching the selector
The root html element in every case
questions.explanation: closest walks upward from the element itself and returns the first match or null. It does not search descendants or siblings, and it only returns html when html actually matches the selector.

questions.question: What is visual hierarchy in user interface design?
options: Arranging elements so the most important ones are noticed first through size, contrast, and placement.
A technique for sorting database rows.
Assigning random z-index values to layers.
A method of compressing responsive images.
questions.explanation: Visual hierarchy guides attention using size, colour, spacing, and position so key content stands out. It is not a database concept, arbitrary layering, or an image compression technique.

questions.question: What does Fitts's Law predict about pointing tasks?
options: That colour contrast determines reading speed.
That larger font files always load more slowly.
That users always prefer dark themes.
That the time to acquire a target depends on its size and distance.
questions.explanation: Fitts's Law models movement time as a function of target size and distance to it, guiding button sizing and placement. It makes no claims about contrast, font loading, or theme preference.

questions.question: What is an affordance in interface design?
options: A visual or functional cue that suggests how an object can be used.
questions.explanation: An affordance communicates possible actions, such as a raised button suggesting it can be pressed. It is not a permission system, animation type, or security credential.

questions.question: Which usability heuristic says the system should keep users informed about what is happening?
questions.explanation: Visibility of system status calls for timely feedback such as progress indicators. User control is about undo and exit, minimalism about irrelevant content, and progressive disclosure about revealing detail gradually.

questions.question: What is a wireframe?
options: A low-fidelity schematic of page structure and content placement.
questions.explanation: A wireframe sketches layout, hierarchy, and placement without visual polish so structure can be evaluated early. It is not CSS, a testing tool, or a data model diagram.

questions.question: What is a prototype in UX design?
options: An interactive or static model of a design used to test ideas before implementation.
A compiled executable delivered to users.
questions.explanation: A prototype lets designers and users explore behaviour and flow before expensive development. It is not a compiled binary, a reset sheet, or server configuration.

questions.question: Which colour model uses cyan, magenta, yellow, and key (black) components?
questions.explanation: CMYK is the subtractive model used in printing. RGB, HSL, and HSV are screen-oriented models based on light, hue, saturation, and brightness.

questions.question: What does a high-contrast text and background pair primarily improve?
options: Readability and accessibility for users with low vision
questions.explanation: Strong contrast makes text legible for people with low vision and in poor viewing conditions. It does not speed up servers, guarantee rankings, or change browser support.

questions.question: What is a design system?
options: A reusable collection of components, tokens, patterns, and guidelines for consistent design.
A CSS framework that can never be customised.
questions.explanation: A design system codifies reusable components and decisions so products stay consistent and teams move faster. It is not one page, an unchangeable library, or a management method.

questions.question: Which choice most directly improves the legibility of long-form body text?
options: Setting all text in capital letters
Choosing decorative display typefaces for paragraphs
Using a readable body font size with comfortable line-height and measure
questions.explanation: Adequate size, generous but not excessive leading, and a sensible line length make paragraphs readable. All caps, cramped lines, and decorative faces all slow reading.

questions.question: What is a loading state in an interface?
options: A visual indication that an operation is still in progress.
A CSS media query for large screens.
An index in a database table.
questions.explanation: A loading state such as a spinner or skeleton reassures users that work is happening. It is not an error endpoint, a responsive rule, or a storage structure.

questions.question: What is usability testing?
options: Observing real users attempting tasks to discover usability problems.
Running unit tests against JavaScript functions.
Checking whether HTML tags are syntactically valid.
questions.explanation: Usability testing watches representative users perform realistic tasks to reveal friction points. Server metrics, unit tests, and markup validators answer different questions about the product.

questions.question: What is natural mapping in interface design?
options: Randomising the order of menu items.
Generating layouts automatically without a designer.
Designing controls so their relationship to the outcome is obvious and mirrors real-world expectations.
questions.explanation: Natural mapping makes the connection between a control and its effect immediately clear, like a switch that looks like the appliance it controls. Arbitrary icons, random order, and auto-generation do the opposite.

questions.question: What does Hick's Law state?
options: Decision time grows with the number and complexity of available choices.
Larger targets are always slower to acquire.
Users can remember exactly seven items in working memory.
Colour choice has no effect on interfaces.
questions.explanation: Hick's Law describes the logarithmic increase in choice reaction time as options multiply, supporting simpler menus. Fitts's Law concerns targeting, the 7±2 claim is a different memory heuristic, and colour research is separate.

questions.question: Which practice reflects progressive disclosure?
options: Showing every advanced option at once by default.
Hiding the primary call to action.
Presenting only essential information first and revealing details on demand.
Disabling all navigation until the user logs in.
questions.explanation: Progressive disclosure reduces overload by revealing advanced controls only when needed. Showing everything immediately, hiding primary actions, or blocking navigation are not the principle.

questions.question: What is the role of a style guide within a design system?
options: Listing database indexes and query plans.
Defining consistent typography, colour, spacing, and component usage rules.
Replacing the need for any usability research.
questions.explanation: A style guide records visual and interaction decisions so implementations stay coherent. It is not infrastructure documentation, a database artefact, or a substitute for testing with users.

questions.question: Which colour scheme uses colours next to each other on the colour wheel?
questions.explanation: Analogous schemes use neighbouring hues for a harmonious look. Complementary hues sit opposite, triadic schemes use three evenly spaced hues, and monochromatic uses one hue with varied lightness.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a call-to-action button?
options: Navigating to the homepage under all circumstances.
Listing every available option at once.
Prompting the user to take one specific desired action.
questions.explanation: A CTA focuses attention on a single next step such as Sign up or Buy now. It is not for legal text, generic home navigation, or presenting an exhaustive menu.

questions.question: Which measures best indicate how easily users complete tasks in a usability test?
options: Task success rate and time on task.
The number of CSS rules in the stylesheet.
questions.explanation: Task completion and efficiency directly reflect usability, unlike performance scores, CSS counts, or bundle sizes, which measure technical qualities rather than user outcomes.

questions.question: What is cognitive load in the context of interface design?
options: The amount of RAM used by the browser.
The mental effort required to understand and use an interface.
The number of network requests a page makes.
The CPU utilisation of a mobile device.
questions.explanation: Cognitive load describes how much thinking a user must do to interact with a product. Memory use, network requests, and CPU load are technical performance measures instead.

questions.question: Which practice makes error messages genuinely helpful?
options: Displaying only a generic code such as Error 500.
Holding back all error information from users.
Blaming the user without offering a next step.
Explaining in plain language what happened and how to recover.
questions.explanation: Good errors describe the problem and a recovery path in user language. Opaque codes, silence, and blame leave users unable to fix the situation.

questions.question: What is card sorting used for in information architecture?
options: Learning how users mentally group content to inform navigation and labels.
Testing the performance of CSS Grid layouts.
Measuring page load time on mobile networks.
Writing automated tests for JavaScript modules.
questions.explanation: Participants group topic cards, revealing mental models that guide navigation structure and terminology. It does not test CSS, network speed, or code correctness.

questions.question: Which spacing practice creates visual rhythm and groups related elements?
options: Choosing a different random margin for each component.
Removing all whitespace from the layout.
Using a consistent spacing scale and tokens.
Relying only on borders to separate content.
questions.explanation: A shared spacing scale produces consistent grouping and rhythm across screens. Random margins, no whitespace, and border-only separation create confused or cramped layouts.

questions.question: What does 'above the fold' refer to in web design?
options: The first lines of the HTML source file.
A CSS positioning technique for fixed headers.
The content visible before the user scrolls on initial view.
questions.explanation: The phrase describes what a visitor sees immediately without scrolling, so key messages belong there. It is not about source order, a CSS trick, or exception handling.

questions.question: Which factor most influences whether a control is perceived as clickable?
options: Visual cues such as shape, colour, shadow, and a clear label.
The number of CSS files loaded.
The domain name of the website.
The rendering engine used by the browser.
questions.explanation: Perceived affordances like button shape, contrast, and labelling signal interactivity. File count, domain, and engine do not communicate that an element can be clicked.

questions.question: Which combination best reduces errors in a long, complex form?
options: Placing every field on one screen with no guidance.
Removing all validation feedback until final submission.
Using colour alone to mark invalid fields.
Clear labels, inline validation, sensible defaults, and confirmation for destructive actions.
questions.explanation: Clear labels, timely validation, defaults, and confirmation prevent and catch mistakes. Overloading one screen, delaying feedback, and relying only on colour all increase user errors.

questions.question: What is a key drawback of using a hamburger menu for primary navigation on desktop?
options: It cannot be styled with CSS at all.
It hides navigation options, reducing discoverability and raising interaction cost.
It makes the website load from a different server.
It always violates HTML validity rules.
questions.explanation: Concealing primary destinations behind an icon makes them less visible and adds a click, harming discoverability. It is styleable, valid HTML, and has no hosting implications.

questions.question: Which statement about skeleton screens compared with spinners is most accurate?
options: Spinners always reduce perceived waiting more than skeletons.
Skeletons can reduce perceived waiting by showing page structure early, but must resemble the content that arrives.
Skeletons and spinners are identical patterns with different colours.
Skeletons eliminate the real network load time.
questions.explanation: Skeletons set expectations about upcoming layout and can feel faster, but misleading shapes cause surprise. Neither pattern changes actual load time, and spinners are not universally better.

questions.question: Which research method best explains why users struggle with a checkout flow?
options: Counting total page views in analytics.
Moderated usability testing with a think-aloud protocol.
questions.explanation: Think-aloud sessions expose the reasoning and confusion behind behaviour, which quantitative metrics and automated audits cannot explain on their own.

questions.question: What does the Zeigarnik effect sometimes motivate in UX design?
options: People remember unfinished tasks better, supporting progress indicators and saved drafts.
Users always prefer the longest possible page.
Nobody can read more than ten words at a time.
Colour has no measurable effect on behaviour.
questions.explanation: The tendency to recall interrupted tasks more vividly is used to justify visible progress and resumable work. It says nothing about page length, a ten-word reading limit, or colour irrelevance.

questions.question: Which design choice supports both novice and expert users?
options: Removing every label so the screen stays minimal for experts.
Offering only keyboard shortcuts with no visible controls.
Clear defaults and shortcuts for experts alongside discoverable labelled controls for novices.
Hiding all help content from every user.
questions.explanation: Layered support gives beginners guidance while letting experienced users work quickly with accelerators. Removing labels, shortcuts only, or hiding help excludes one group or both.

questions.question: What does WCAG stand for?
questions.explanation: WCAG is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines published by the W3C. The other expansions are invented phrases that do not name any recognised standard.

questions.question: Which WCAG conformance level represents the minimum level of accessibility?
questions.explanation: Level A contains the most basic success criteria, with AA addressing major barriers and AAA adding stricter requirements. A+ is not a conformance level.

questions.question: What is the minimum WCAG AA contrast ratio for normal-sized text?
questions.explanation: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Ratios of 2:1 and 4:1 fall short of the requirement, and 3:1 applies only to large text or non-text UI components.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute supplies a text alternative for an image?
questions.explanation: alt provides the accessible text alternative for img elements and is read by screen readers. title is only a tooltip, aria-label is a fallback rather than the primary mechanism, and placeholder is for form hints.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of ARIA?
options: Supplying roles, states, and properties to assistive technology when native HTML is insufficient.
Compressing image files for the web.
Validating CSS syntax at build time.
questions.explanation: ARIA fills semantic gaps for custom widgets by exposing roles and states to the accessibility tree. It does not style, compress media, or validate stylesheets.

questions.question: Which ARIA role marks a navigation landmark?
questions.explanation: role='navigation' identifies a navigation landmark equivalent to the nav element. banner, main, and contentinfo correspond to header, main, and footer landmarks instead.

questions.question: Which key normally activates a focused button or link?
questions.explanation: Enter activates links and buttons from the keyboard; Space also activates buttons. Escape typically closes dialogs, Tab moves focus, and Shift modifies Tab direction.

questions.question: Which key moves keyboard focus to the next focusable element?
questions.explanation: Tab advances focus through focusable elements in DOM order, with Shift+Tab going backward. Enter and Space activate controls, while Alt is a modifier key.

questions.question: What does a visible focus indicator communicate?
options: That a tooltip is about to appear.
That the page title has changed.
Which element currently has keyboard focus.
That the element has been permanently hidden.
questions.explanation: A focus ring shows keyboard users where they are on the page, which is essential for orientation. It does not signal tooltips, title changes, or hiding.

questions.question: Which HTML element provides an accessible name for a text input?
questions.explanation: A label associated via for and id gives a control its accessible name and enlarges the click target. div, span, and br have no implicit labelling relationship.

questions.question: What does aria-hidden='true' do?
options: Hides the element visually using display:none.
Makes the element part of the tab order.
Adds a helpful tooltip to the element.
Removes the element and its descendants from the accessibility tree while leaving it visually rendered.
questions.explanation: aria-hidden hides content from assistive technology without changing visual presentation. It does not set CSS display, add focusability, or generate tooltips, and must never be used on focusable content.

questions.question: What is a screen reader?
options: A tool that measures page loading speed.
Software that converts screen content to speech or braille for blind and low-vision users.
A browser extension that sets dark mode.
questions.explanation: A screen reader announces document structure and text through speech or a braille display. It is not a performance tool, theme extension, or image optimiser.

questions.question: Which technique hides content visually while keeping it available to screen readers?
options: Applying display: none to the element.
Using a visually-hidden utility based on clipping and absolute positioning.
