Applying visibility: hidden to the element.
questions.explanation: A clip-based visually-hidden class removes content from view but keeps it in the accessibility tree. display:none, visibility:hidden, and aria-hidden all remove it from assistive technology.

questions.question: Which ARIA attribute reports whether a disclosure control is expanded?
questions.explanation: aria-expanded communicates the open or closed state of a disclosure, combobox, or tree item. aria-hidden hides content, aria-selected marks selection, and aria-checked reports checkbox or radio state.

questions.question: What is the first rule of ARIA?
options: Prefer native HTML semantics and use ARIA only when native elements cannot express the needed meaning.
Add an ARIA role to every single element on the page.
ARIA can replace keyboard event handling entirely.
questions.explanation: Native elements already provide semantics, focus behaviour, and keyboard support, so ARIA should only fill genuine gaps. Adding roles everywhere, avoiding all ARIA in forms, or assuming it supplies keyboard behaviour are misconceptions.

questions.question: Which attribute links an inline validation message to the form control it describes?
questions.explanation: aria-describedby points to elements that provide extra descriptive text such as errors or hints. aria-labelledby provides the accessible name, aria-controls names a controlled element, and aria-owns changes parentage.

questions.question: What is a skip link?
options: A link that clears all cookies.
A link that always opens the next page in a sequence.
A link near the start of the page that lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation.
A link that triggers a hard reload.
questions.explanation: A skip link targets main content so keyboard and screen reader users do not traverse the same navigation on every page. It does not clear data, page forward, or reload the site.

questions.question: Which markup correctly groups related radio buttons with a group label?
options: A fieldset element containing a legend and the radio inputs
A div containing a label and the radio inputs
A section containing a caption and the radio inputs
A form containing a title and the radio inputs
questions.explanation: fieldset with legend gives the radio group a programmatic group name exposed to assistive technology. A plain div label, a table caption, and a document title do not group form controls.

questions.question: What does role='alert' communicate to assistive technology?
options: That the content is purely decorative.
That the content is a navigation landmark.
That the content should be hidden from assistive technology.
That the content is an important, time-sensitive message to announce immediately.
questions.explanation: role='alert' is an assertive live region for urgent messages such as errors. It is not decorative, not a landmark, and the opposite of hidden from assistive technology.

questions.question: Which contrast ratio is the WCAG AA requirement for large text?
questions.explanation: Large text, roughly 24px or 18.66px bold, needs at least 3:1 at AA; normal text needs 4.5:1. Level AAA raises these thresholds, while 2:1 is insufficient.

questions.question: Which attribute gives an iframe an accessible name?
questions.explanation: title supplies an accessible name for the embedded frame so users know what it contains. name identifies a browsing context target, alt applies to images, and aria-hidden removes the frame from the accessibility tree.

questions.question: What does the required attribute communicate about a form control?
options: Nothing; it is a purely visual styling hint.
That the control cannot be edited by the user.
That entered text must be uppercase.
That the field is mandatory, typically exposed as aria-required to assistive technology.
questions.explanation: required participates in constraint validation and is mapped to an accessible required state. It does not style the field, make it read-only, or transform text casing.

questions.question: Why should colour never be the only way to convey information?
options: Users with colour vision deficiencies or monochrome displays may not perceive the distinction.
Colour is not supported by modern CSS.
It always increases the size of the HTML file.
Screen readers cannot render any colours at all.
questions.explanation: Colour blind users, people using high-contrast modes, and monochrome output can miss colour-only cues, so add text, icons, or patterns. CSS supports colour fully, file size is irrelevant, and the issue is perception rather than screen reader rendering.

questions.question: Which aria-live value announces updates politely once the user is idle?
questions.explanation: polite queues announcements until the screen reader finishes its current speech. off suppresses updates, assertive interrupts immediately, and 'now' is not a valid aria-live value.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the caption element inside a data table?
options: Adding a CSS caption to the table border.
Hiding the table from screen reader users.
Providing an accessible name or description for the table.
Sorting the rows automatically by the first column.
questions.explanation: caption names the table for assistive technology and sighted users alike. It does not style borders, hide content, or perform any sorting of table data.

questions.question: Which statement about tabindex and focus order is correct?
options: Positive tabindex values override natural DOM order and are generally discouraged; prefer DOM order with 0 or -1.
Every focusable element must use tabindex='1'.
tabindex='-1' puts the element first in the tab sequence.
Focus order can never be influenced by markup or CSS.
questions.explanation: Positive tabindex creates a separate, confusing tab sequence, so authors should rely on DOM order and use 0 for custom focusability or -1 for programmatic focus. Tab indices are not mandatory, -1 is not first, and markup strongly affects order.

questions.question: Why must a custom control built from a div add role, tabindex, and keyboard handlers?
options: Because div elements cannot be styled with CSS.
Because adding an ARIA role automatically supplies keyboard behaviour.
Because screen readers ignore all native HTML elements.
Because native semantics and focusability are absent, so the author must provide them.
questions.explanation: A div conveys no role, is not focusable, and has no built-in key handling, so all three must be supplied to emulate a button. CSS styling is unrelated, roles do not add behaviour, and native elements are fully exposed.

questions.question: What does aria-labelledby='title' do when an element with id title exists?
options: Adds a browser tooltip on hover.
Uses that element's text as the accessible name of the current element.
Hides the referenced label visually in every case.
questions.explanation: aria-labelledby builds the accessible name from the text of referenced elements, which is useful when a visible heading labels a region. It is not a tooltip mechanism, does not hide the label, and has no form submission role.

questions.question: Which statement about contrast ratio calculation is correct?
options: Contrast ratio is measured in CSS pixels.
It compares the relative luminance of foreground and background on a scale from 1:1 to 21:1.
It is relevant only for photographs.
It is calculated from the size of the font file.
questions.explanation: WCAG contrast ratio uses relative luminance, with black on white reaching 21:1 and identical colours 1:1. It is unitless, applies to text and UI components, and has nothing to do with font file size.

questions.question: How is the accessible name determined for a button with both aria-label and visible text?
options: Visible text always takes precedence over aria-label.
aria-label is always ignored when text is present.
The accessible name is always empty for such a button.
aria-label generally overrides the text content, so it should repeat the visible label to satisfy label-in-name.
questions.explanation: The accessible name computation gives aria-label priority over content, so a mismatched label can break voice control. Repeating the visible words avoids that problem; text does not always win, nor is aria-label ignored.

questions.question: How should a page support users who prefer reduced motion?
options: Honour prefers-reduced-motion by disabling or shortening non-essential animation.
Remove every animation globally, including essential ones, with no conditions.
Ignore the media query because it only controls audio playback.
questions.explanation: The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets optional movement be suppressed while essential feedback can remain. Forcing removal for everyone is excessive, longer animation is unhelpful, and the query affects visual motion.

questions.question: What does LCP stand for among the Core Web Vitals?
questions.explanation: Largest Contentful Paint records when the largest image or text block in the viewport renders. The other phrases are invented expansions with no meaning in web performance.

questions.question: Which Core Web Vital measures visual stability during page loading?
questions.explanation: Cumulative Layout Shift quantifies unexpected movement of visible elements. LCP measures loading of the largest element, INP responsiveness, and FCP when the first content appears.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute defers loading of offscreen images until they are near the viewport?
questions.explanation: loading='lazy' lets the browser postpone image or iframe requests until they are close to being visible. defer and async are script attributes, while preload is a link relationship for early fetching.

questions.question: Which script attribute waits until HTML parsing finishes and then runs scripts in document order?
questions.explanation: defer downloads without blocking parsing, executes after parsing in order, and fires before DOMContentLoaded. async executes as soon as it arrives regardless of order, and immediate is not an attribute.

questions.question: What is minification in a front-end build?
options: Converting bitmap images into vector graphics.
Removing whitespace and comments and shortening identifiers without changing behaviour.
Compressing all server responses with gzip only.
Deleting unused pages from the project.
questions.explanation: Minification shrinks CSS and JavaScript text by stripping formatting and renaming identifiers while preserving behaviour. Vector conversion, transport compression, and removing pages are separate concerns.

questions.question: Which HTTP response header specifies how long a resource may be cached?
questions.explanation: Cache-Control directives such as max-age define caching policy. Content-Type declares media type, Set-Cookie stores session data, and Authorization carries credentials.

questions.question: Which build optimisation removes unused exported code from the final bundle?
questions.explanation: Tree shaking analyses static module dependencies and drops exports that are never used. Minification only shortens syntax, caching stores responses, and lazy loading defers loading at runtime.

questions.question: What is a service worker?
options: A script running in the background that intercepts network requests for caching and offline support.
A CSS preprocessor for nesting rules.
A DOM event handler attached to a form.
questions.explanation: A service worker is a worker script scoped to an origin that can intercept fetches and use the Cache API. It is not a preprocessor, event handler, or database process.

questions.question: What does PWA stand for?
questions.explanation: PWA means Progressive Web App, a web experience using service workers, manifests, and HTTPS for app-like behaviour. The other expansions are not standard terms.

questions.question: Which browser DevTools panel lists requests with status codes and timings?
questions.explanation: The Network panel records each request, its headers, status, size, and timeline. Elements inspects DOM and CSS, Sources debugs scripts, and Performance profiles runtime work.

questions.question: Which Git command creates a new branch?
questions.explanation: git branch <name> creates a branch pointer; git checkout -b also creates and switches. commit records changes, push uploads refs, and merge combines branches.

questions.question: Which npm command installs a package as a development dependency?
questions.explanation: The --save-dev flag adds the package to devDependencies, used only during development. -g installs globally, start runs a script, and remove uninstalls a package.

questions.question: What happens during the render-tree stage of the critical rendering path?
options: A DNS lookup resolves the origin hostname.
The DOM and CSSOM combine into a render tree before layout and paint.
Unused memory is reclaimed by garbage collection.
A service worker is registered with the browser.
questions.explanation: The browser builds the DOM and CSSOM, combines visible nodes into a render tree, computes layout, then paints and composites. DNS, garbage collection, and worker registration are unrelated stages.

questions.question: What does <link rel='preload'> tell the browser?
options: To postpone script execution until the window loads.
To fetch and cache a resource early because it will be needed soon.
To install a fallback font automatically.
To stop rendering until the resource arrives.
questions.explanation: preload is a hint that starts an early high-priority fetch for a known resource such as a hero font. It does not defer scripts, install fonts by itself, or block rendering.

questions.question: Which Core Web Vital replaced First Input Delay as the responsiveness metric?
questions.explanation: Interaction to Next Paint measures latency across interactions and replaced FID in 2024. LCP covers loading, CLS covers stability, and TTFB measures server response start.

questions.question: Which image attributes help reserve space and prevent layout shift before loading?
questions.explanation: Width and height let the browser infer the aspect ratio and reserve a box before bytes arrive. Eager loading, decoding hints, and alt text do not reserve layout space.

questions.question: What is code splitting?
options: Stripping all comments out of source files.
Combining every script into one large bundle.
Dividing a bundle into smaller chunks that can be loaded on demand.
Converting all CSS into inline style attributes.
questions.explanation: Code splitting creates smaller chunks, often per route or feature, so users download what they need first. Minification strips text, bundling merges files, and inlining CSS is unrelated.

questions.question: Which tool is primarily a JavaScript module bundler?
questions.explanation: webpack resolves module imports and produces bundles. Babel transpiles syntax, ESLint checks code quality, and Git tracks versions.

questions.question: Which animation approach usually avoids costly layout work?
questions.explanation: Transform and opacity can often be handled by the compositor without layout or paint. Animating width, left, margins, or large shadows typically triggers reflow or repaint.

questions.question: What does content-visibility: auto do for offscreen content?
options: Deletes the elements from the DOM.
Disables all CSS for those elements.
Forces immediate rendering of everything offscreen.
Skips much of the rendering work until the content approaches the viewport.
questions.explanation: content-visibility:auto lets the browser skip layout and painting for offscreen subtrees while keeping them in the DOM. It does not delete nodes, disable styles, or force early rendering.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the ETag response header?
options: Setting the exact expiry date of a cached resource.
Providing a resource version so the browser can validate its cached copy with a conditional request.
Compressing image files on the server.
questions.explanation: ETag identifies a resource version used with If-None-Match; an unchanged resource returns 304 Not Modified. Expiry comes from Cache-Control or Expires, and compression or cookie signing are different features.

questions.question: Which DevTools feature records CPU activity and frame timing to diagnose jank?
options: A recording in the Performance panel
questions.explanation: The Performance panel captures scripting, layout, paint, and frame data over time. Application manages storage and manifests, Console logs messages, and throttling only simulates networks.

questions.question: Which @font-face descriptor renders text with a fallback while a web font downloads?
questions.explanation: font-display:swap uses a fallback immediately and swaps in the downloaded face, keeping text visible. font-display:block briefly hides text, while font-weight and font-style describe the face itself.

questions.question: Which Git command stages all changed and new files for the next commit?
questions.explanation: git add -A stages additions, modifications, and deletions across the whole tree. commit -am only stages tracked modified files, checkout switches refs, and stash shelves changes.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts async and defer for classic scripts?
options: async always preserves document order of execution.
async executes as soon as downloaded and may run before parsing finishes; defer waits for parsing and preserves order.
defer blocks HTML parsing until the script finishes downloading.
questions.explanation: async removes ordering guarantees and can run mid-parse, while defer waits until parsing completes and then runs in order. Both download without blocking, so neither guarantees post-DOMContentLoaded execution in every case.

questions.question: Why can a very large hero image produce a poor Largest Contentful Paint score?
options: Because LCP only measures JavaScript execution time.
Because LCP completely ignores images in the viewport.
Because LCP records the render time of the largest viewport image or text block, so slow delivery delays it.
Because LCP counts only the number of network requests.
questions.explanation: LCP is the paint time of the largest contentful element, often a hero image, so late loading or late insertion directly worsens it. It is not a JS-only metric, does not ignore images, and is not a request count.

questions.question: What is the purpose of font-display: optional?
options: It gives the font a very short block period and may skip the web font on slow connections to avoid layout shift.
It always swaps the font in after exactly three seconds.
It disables all fallback font faces.
It preloads every font declared in the stylesheet.
questions.explanation: optional keeps the block phase tiny and can leave the fallback in place when the font is not ready, prioritising stability over a font swap. It is not a fixed three-second timer, does not disable fallbacks, and does not preload.

questions.question: Which strategy best reduces INP caused by a long click handler?
options: Increasing the duration of the click animation.
Wrapping all work in setTimeout with a five-second delay.
Moving every task into one larger synchronous function.
Splitting work into smaller tasks, yielding to the main thread, and deferring non-urgent work.
questions.explanation: Breaking up long tasks lets the browser paint and respond between chunks, improving Interaction to Next Paint. Longer animations, arbitrary five-second delays, and bigger synchronous blocks all make responsiveness worse.

questions.question: Which statement about HTTP/2 multiplexing is accurate?
options: It requires a separate TCP connection for every resource.
It allows multiple request and response streams over one connection, reducing application-layer head-of-line blocking.
It is a feature exclusive to HTTP/1.1.
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 interleaves many streams on a single connection, so one slow response does not block others at the application layer. It does not open a connection per asset, disable caching, or belong to HTTP/1.1.

questions.question: What does a service worker's fetch event handler typically do?
options: Intercepts requests and answers from the Cache API or forwards them to the network.
Compiles JavaScript into WebAssembly on the fly.
Changes the DOM of the current page directly.
questions.explanation: The fetch event lets a service worker implement cache-first or network-first strategies for offline support. It does not minify assets, compile WebAssembly, or access the page DOM directly.

questions.question: What does tree shaking rely on to work effectively?
options: Using the window global everywhere in the code.
Exclusively using CommonJS dynamic require calls.
Applying minification alone to the source files.
ES module syntax with static imports so the bundler can identify unused exports.
questions.explanation: Static ES import and export statements let a bundler build a dependency graph and safely drop unreachable code. Dynamic CommonJS requires, global usage, and minification alone do not provide that analysis.
